newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada sees low inflation through 1996.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada sees low inflation through 1996.

text.p: Bank of Canada governor Gordon Thiessen said a wide output gap in Canada's economy was the main factor behind Canada's low inflation.

"The sizable margin of slack in the economy was the main factor exerting downward pressure on inflation," Thiessen said in remarks to the Bank's September 5 Board of Directors meeting, released on Wednesday.
He said inflation was expected to stay in the lower half of the bank's 1-3 percent target range for the remainder of 1996.
The Bank's minutes also said that international economic conditions remained very positive for Canada.

"World prices for many of the primary products that Canada exports remain at high levels, and our two morst important trading partners, the United States and Japan, have been experiencing strong growth," the Bank's minutes said.
But the Bank added that there was a risk the U.S. economy might grow too quickly, causing inflationary pressure.
"A tighter monetary policy stance may thus be required to offset these pressures and to help sustain U.S. economic growth over the medium term," the Bank said.

Noting that domestic demand in Canada remained weak in recent quarters, the Bank said it expected growth to pick up in the second half of 1996, supported by increased consumer spending, a rebound in business investment and continued strength in exports.
"There are nevertheless a number of signs pointing to a pickup in the pace of economic activity in Canada in the second half of 1996," the Bank said.

The Bank said recent fiscal policy adjustments, a dramatic improvement in Canada's current account and low domestic inflation had given strength to the Canadian dollar and had allowed the Bank to ease interest rates several times over the past two months.
